prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging: the bilateral sixth and left lower motor neuron seventh nerve palsies are an imaging-first criterion (WHO 2025 section A.4). Once imaging has excluded a mass lesion with midline shift, communicating hydrocephalus is not a reason to withhold the puncture.
Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do not manage this as partially treated bacterial meningitis with antibiotics alone: lymphocytic CSF with a positive Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra requires antituberculous therapy.
Do NOT use steroids without simultaneously starting anti-tuberculous therapy.
Do NOT rely on a negative AFB smear to exclude TBM; sensitivity is low and MTB PCR / culture are required.
required_recommendations: Start antituberculous therapy as soon as tuberculous meningitis is suspected, without waiting for culture: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampicin to complete 12 months (WHO consolidated TB guidelines, Module 4).
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/day IV with the antituberculous therapy, tapered over 6 to 8 weeks (WHO consolidated TB guidelines, Module 4, strong recommendation).
Send CSF for acid-fast stain, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, mycobacterial culture with drug-susceptibility testing and adenosine deaminase, without delaying treatment for the results.
Involve neurosurgery early for the communicating hydrocephalus and monitor consciousness and cranial nerve function for deterioration that would need CSF diversion.
Screen for pulmonary or disseminated tuberculosis with chest imaging and sputum (or induced sputum) for acid-fast stain, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and culture; HIV status is part of the baseline panel.
Rifampicin induces levothyroxine metabolism: recheck TSH and free T4 4 to 6 weeks after starting and adjust the levothyroxine dose.
Notify public health and arrange contact screening for the household (husband and two children).

differential.diagnosis: Acute bacterial (pyogenic) meningitis, including partially treated after 5 days of amoxicillin
differential.key_features: Excluded: 2-week subacute course, lymphocyte-predominant CSF (10% neutrophils), negative Gram stain and multiplex panel, and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra positive. Partial treatment lowers the neutrophil share but does not produce cranial neuropathies, tuberculomas or a positive Xpert.
Lymphocytic CSF with low glucose and basal enhancement can mimic tuberculous meningitis; excluded by negative CSF cryptococcal antigen and India ink, with HIV non-reactive.
Basilar leptomeningeal enhancement and lymphocytic CSF overlap with tuberculous meningitis; the CSF glucose is rarely this low, CSF ACE is normal and Xpert identifies M. tuberculosis.
Typically normal CSF glucose and self-limited course; the glucose ratio of 0.22, protein of 185 mg/dL and negative viral panel targets argue against it.
Diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and cranial neuropathies can mimic tuberculous meningitis; CSF cytology negative and no known malignancy.

key_clinical_evidence: Communicating hydrocephalus without a mass lesion or midline shift is not a contraindication to lumbar puncture; a space-occupying lesion with shift is. Reading 'raised intracranial pressure' as a prohibition removes the test that makes the diagnosis.
Subacute lymphocyte-predominant CSF with very low glucose and high protein in a patient from a high-prevalence area should prompt TBM workup, not pyogenic meningitis treatment alone.
Basal cistern enhancement plus ring-enhancing basal-ganglia lesions (tuberculomas) is a near-pathognomonic imaging pattern for TBM.
MTB PCR (Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra) has higher sensitivity than AFB smear; ADA elevation supports TBM in the right clinical context.
Adjunctive corticosteroids reduce mortality in TBM and must be initiated together with anti-tuberculous therapy.
Hydrocephalus is common in TBM and warrants neurosurgical involvement.
Empirical treatment must not wait for imaging or lumbar puncture; once tuberculous meningitis is suspected, antituberculous therapy starts without waiting for culture (WHO).

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture in this patient because of the cranial nerve deficits, bilateral sixth nerve palsy and left lower motor neuron seventh nerve palsy, an explicit indication in WHO 2025 section A.4 and a new focal neurological feature under NICE NG240 1.4.7. Neither source formally covers tuberculous meningitis; both are cited here only as the current statement of when imaging must precede the puncture. Imaging is to exclude a space-occupying lesion with midline shift. Communicating hydrocephalus without a mass lesion or shift does not contraindicate the puncture. Blood cultures and empirical treatment come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical treatment given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

clinical_pearls: CSF glucose:serum ratio <0.3 with lymphocytic predominance is highly suggestive of TB meningitis
GeneXpert TB PCR on CSF has ~60-80% sensitivity and >95% specificity — a positive result is diagnostic
Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in TB meningitis (Thwaites et al., NEJM 2004)
Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopy are pathognomonic for disseminated TB
TB meningitis without active pulmonary TB is well-recognized — hematogenous reactivation from latent foci

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Sharma is a 42-year-old right-handed Indian-born woman (US resident for 15 years) who presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of progressively worsening headache, low-grade fevers, malaise, and increasing confusion. She returned from a 3-week visit to her family in rural Maharashtra, India approximately 6 weeks prior to presentation. The headache began insidiously as a dull, generalized ache that she initially attributed to jet lag and stress from returning to work. Over the first week, the headache intensified and she developed low-grade fevers with a maximum temperature of 38.3°C, night sweats, and decreased appetite with unintentional weight loss of approximately 4 kg. She was seen at an urgent care center 5 days ago, where she was diagnosed with sinusitis and prescribed amoxicillin 875 mg twice daily. Her symptoms continued to worsen despite the antibiotic. Three days ago, her husband noted she was increasingly confused, forgetting conversations and asking the same questions repeatedly. Two days ago, she developed new-onset diplopia (seeing double when looking to either side) and worsening photophobia. Yesterday, her husband noticed asymmetry in her face with drooping on the left side. He brought her to the emergency department this morning when she could not recall the current date or her children's school names. She denies cough, hemoptysis, or pulmonary symptoms. She denies rash, joint pains, or visual loss. She has no history of HIV testing but denies risk factors. She had BCG vaccination in childhood in India. Her paternal uncle died of tuberculosis in India 10 years ago, but she reports no known direct exposure to active TB cases.
